title: Best Foods for a Hangover: What to Eat (and Avoid) the Morning After
excerpt: The best foods for a hangover, grouped by what they actually fix: low blood sugar, lost fluid and salt, and an upset stomach. Plus breakfast ideas, the greasy food myth, and what to avoid.
metaDescription: The best foods for a hangover, sorted by what they fix: blood sugar, fluids, and an upset stomach. Breakfast ideas, the greasy food myth, what to avoid.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best foods for a hangover are the ones that fix the specific things alcohol knocked out of balance: low blood sugar, lost fluid and salt, and an irritated stomach. That means plain carbohydrates like toast, crackers, oatmeal, or rice; salty, watery foods like broth and soup; potassium-rich foods like bananas and avocado; and a little easy protein, such as eggs. No food cures a hangover. There is no good evidence from human trials that any single food makes a hangover end sooner. But eating the right thing at the right time can make the morning noticeably more bearable, and eating the wrong thing (a huge greasy fry-up on a queasy stomach, say) can make it worse.

**The quick plan for this morning:** start with water or an electrolyte drink, in small sips if you feel sick. Once your stomach settles, have something bland and starchy, like two slices of toast, a few crackers, or a bowl of oatmeal. Add a banana or some broth for potassium and salt. When you feel ready for a real meal, eggs on toast or a bowl of soup with noodles and vegetables is a solid choice. Save the heavy, greasy, or spicy food for another day.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is miserable but fades within a day. Get medical help if you or someone else **can't keep any fluids down for several hours**, **vomits blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, has **severe or worsening stomach pain**, is **confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake**, has **a seizure**, or has **slow or irregular breathing**. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning, severe dehydration, or a stomach problem that food won't fix. In an emergency, call 911. If you have diabetes and take insulin or a medicine that lowers blood sugar, alcohol can cause dangerous lows hours after drinking. Check your levels, eat carbohydrates, and contact your doctor if your readings stay low. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Food Helps a Hangover at All

A hangover isn't one problem. It's a bundle of them, and researchers still argue about which parts matter most. The big contributors seem to be:

- **Inflammation and the immune response.** Alcohol triggers a low-grade inflammatory reaction that a lot of researchers now think drives much of the "poisoned" feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product, before breaking it down further.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more than you drink.
- **Low blood sugar.** While your liver is busy with alcohol, it makes less new glucose. Some people wake up with lower blood sugar than usual, which can add to shakiness, weakness, and fogginess.
- **An irritated stomach.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and irritates the stomach lining, which is why nausea and stomach pain are so common.

Food can't do much about inflammation or sleep. It can help a lot with the last three: fluid and salt, blood sugar, and a stomach that needs something gentle. That's the honest frame for every food on this list. We've grouped them by what they actually do, so you can pick based on how you feel.

## The Best Hangover Foods at a Glance

| Food | What it does | Evidence | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Toast, crackers, plain rice | Quick, gentle carbohydrates for blood sugar | Sound physiology, no hangover trials | Nausea, shakiness, first food of the day |
| Oatmeal | Slower carbs, some fiber, easy to digest | Sound physiology | Steady energy through the morning |
| Bananas | Potassium plus easy carbs | Sound physiology; potassium loss is modest | Mild nausea, low appetite |
| Broth and soup | Fluid plus sodium, warm and gentle | Sound physiology, strong tradition | Dehydration, can't face solid food |
| Eggs | Protein and cysteine | Plausible chemistry, small supplement trial only | A proper breakfast once you can eat |
| Ginger | Settles nausea | Good evidence for nausea in general, little for hangovers | Queasy stomach |
| Watermelon, cucumber, oranges | Water and some potassium | Sound physiology | Thirst, light appetite |
| Avocado, sweet potato, spinach | Potassium and other minerals | Sound physiology | Later meals |
| Coconut water | Fluid and potassium | Small rehydration studies, not hangover-specific | Rehydration if you like the taste |
| Greasy fry-up | Fat and salt, comfort | No good evidence it helps after drinking | Mostly comfort; can worsen reflux |

"Sound physiology" here means the food addresses a real effect of alcohol, but nobody has run a proper trial showing it shortens a hangover. That's true of almost every hangover food, so don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

## Foods That Bring Your Blood Sugar Back Up

When your liver is processing alcohol, it puts less effort into gluconeogenesis, which is its way of making new glucose to keep your blood sugar steady between meals. If you drank on a light dinner and then slept through breakfast, you can wake up low. Studies have measured lower blood sugar in some hungover people, though the link between blood sugar and how bad the hangover feels hasn't been consistent. Either way, getting some carbohydrate into you is one of the simplest things you can do.

### Toast and crackers

Plain toast and saltine crackers are the classic first food for a reason. They're bland, they don't sit heavily, they absorb some stomach acid, and they give you fast carbohydrates. Saltines also bring a little sodium. If you feel sick, nibble a cracker or half a slice of dry toast and wait ten minutes before having more. Butter, honey, or a little jam is fine once you're sure it's staying down.

### Oatmeal

Oatmeal gives you slower-releasing carbohydrates than white toast, so it keeps your energy steadier through the morning. It's soft, warm, and easy to digest. Make it with water or milk, and add a sliced banana or a spoon of honey for flavor and extra quick carbs.

### Plain rice and noodles

White rice, rice porridge (congee), and plain noodles are gentle staples across many cuisines. A bowl of congee or rice in broth combines carbohydrates, salt, and fluid in one easy dish.

### Honey and sugar

A spoon of honey in tea or on toast brings quick sugar. You'll sometimes read that the fructose in honey "speeds up" alcohol metabolism. There's some old research on fructose and alcohol clearance, but the effect in people is small and inconsistent, and there is no good evidence that honey sobers you up or shortens a hangover. Treat it as a pleasant, quick carbohydrate, nothing more.

## Foods That Replace Fluid, Salt, and Potassium

Alcohol makes you pee more, and if you vomited or sweated, you lost more fluid and salt on top of that. Mild dehydration contributes to headache, thirst, dry mouth, and fatigue. It's worth knowing that studies haven't found a strong link between measured electrolyte levels and hangover severity, so don't expect a banana to fix everything. Still, replacing fluid is one of the most reliable ways to feel a bit better.

### Broth and soup

A warm bowl of broth is probably the single best "food" for a rough morning. It's mostly water, it carries sodium (which helps your body hold onto that water), and the warmth is soothing on an upset stomach. Chicken noodle soup, bone broth, miso soup, pho, and ramen are all popular hangover meals in different parts of the world. Our guide to the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) goes through each one, and the [traditional Mexican hangover remedies](/never-hungover/traditional-mexican-hangover-remedies-vs-modern-supplements) guide covers menudo and other classics.

### Bananas

A medium banana has roughly 400 to 450 mg of potassium, along with easy carbohydrates, and it's one of the gentlest foods you can eat when nauseous. That's why it's part of the old "BRAT" diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) for upset stomachs. The potassium story is often overstated: most people don't lose dangerous amounts of potassium from one night of drinking. But a banana is still a smart, easy choice.

### Watermelon, cucumber, and other watery produce

Watermelon is about 90% water and brings a little potassium and sugar. You'll see claims that its citrulline content helps with hangovers. There's no good evidence for that specific claim, but watermelon is refreshing, hydrating, and easy to eat. Cucumber, oranges, grapes, and berries are similar watery choices. If citrus stings an irritated stomach, choose something milder.

### Avocado, sweet potato, and spinach

These are better for your second meal of the day than your first. Avocado actually has more potassium per gram than a banana, and it brings healthy fats that help keep you full. Sweet potatoes and leafy greens also add potassium, magnesium, and other minerals. A bowl of rice with sweet potato and greens, or avocado on toast with an egg, is a good recovery lunch.

### Pickles and pickle juice

Pickle juice is salty, and some people swear by a small glass the morning after. The sodium can help your body retain fluid, but pickle juice is also acidic and can irritate a sensitive stomach. A pickle or two alongside a meal is fine. Gulping a big glass on an empty stomach isn't a great idea if you're already nauseous.

### Coconut water and drinks

Coconut water brings fluid and a good amount of potassium, though it's lower in sodium than a rehydration drink. Our [coconut water for hangovers](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide compares it with sports drinks, and our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) explains which drinks replace fluid best. For a broader list, see our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

## Foods for a Nauseous or Upset Stomach (What to Eat When Hungover and Sick)

If your main problem is nausea, the rule is simple: small amounts, bland food, and patience.

### Start with fluids, then dry carbs

Sip water, an electrolyte drink, or weak tea. If that stays down for 20 to 30 minutes, move on to crackers, dry toast, plain rice, or applesauce. Don't force a full meal. A queasy stomach usually settles faster with a slow start.

### Ginger

Ginger is one of the better-studied natural remedies for nausea, with research in pregnancy-related nausea and nausea after surgery. The evidence for hangovers specifically is thin, but because nausea is nausea, many people find ginger tea, a ginger chew, or real ginger ale helpful. Our [ginger for hangover nausea](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) guide covers what form to use and how much.

### Gentle protein once you can manage it

Once the queasiness fades, a little protein helps you feel more normal. Eggs, plain chicken, yogurt, or tofu are all easy options. For more on settling your stomach, see our full [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## Eggs and Other Protein Foods

Eggs get a special mention because of cysteine. Cysteine is an amino acid that your body uses to make glutathione, one of the liver's main antioxidants, and it can bind acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol. That's real chemistry. A small 2020 Finnish trial found that an L-cysteine supplement taken during drinking was linked to less nausea and headache the next day, though it was a supplement at a fairly high dose, not eggs, and it was a small study.

So eggs aren't a hangover treatment. They're a good recovery breakfast: soft, high in protein, easy to cook, and gentle on most stomachs. Our [eggs for hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) guide explains how much cysteine a serving really contains, and the [L-cysteine for hangovers](/never-hungover/l-cysteine-for-hangover) guide covers the supplement trial in detail.

Other good protein choices the morning after include Greek yogurt (which also brings some fluid), cottage cheese, smoked salmon on toast, a turkey sandwich, or tofu in broth. Lean protein with carbohydrate tends to keep your energy steadier than carbohydrate alone.

## The Best Hangover Breakfast Ideas

If you want simple meals rather than a list of ingredients, these combine the main things a hangover breakfast should do.

1. **Eggs on toast with a banana.** Protein, quick carbs, and potassium. Scramble the eggs softly if your stomach is touchy.
2. **Oatmeal with banana and honey.** Gentle, warm, and steady. Make it with milk for extra protein, or water if dairy feels heavy.
3. **Chicken noodle soup or rice in broth.** Fluid, salt, and carbs in one bowl. Ideal when you can't face anything solid.
4. **Avocado toast with an egg.** A bit more substantial for later in the morning. Potassium, fat, protein, and carbs.
5. **Greek yogurt with berries and granola.** Cold and easy if hot food feels like too much. Add honey for quick sugar.

Pair any of these with a big glass of water, and add an electrolyte drink if you were sick or sweated a lot. Coffee is fine if you normally drink it. Skipping your usual coffee can bring on a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. Just don't use it as a replacement for water.

## Does Greasy Food Help a Hangover?

This is the most common hangover-food myth. Greasy food can help a little, but at the wrong end of the night.

Eating a meal with fat, protein, and carbohydrate *before or while* you drink slows the rate at which alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That means a slower, lower peak in blood alcohol. That's well established, and it's why drinking on an empty stomach hits so hard. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the best pre-drinking meals, and our [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) guide explains why skipping dinner backfires.

The morning after is different. By then the alcohol is already absorbed, so fat can't "soak it up." There is no good evidence that a greasy breakfast speeds recovery. And fatty food slows stomach emptying and can relax the valve at the top of your stomach, which can make nausea and acid reflux worse. If you already have [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking), a plate of bacon and fried bread may not be kind to you.

That said, if a bacon-and-egg sandwich is what you can face and it sits well, the eggs, bread, and salt are doing some real good. The comfort factor matters too. Just don't expect the grease itself to be the cure.

### Does bread soak up alcohol?

Not in the way people imagine. Bread doesn't absorb alcohol like a sponge. Eating before or during drinking slows absorption because food in general keeps alcohol in your stomach longer. Eating bread at the end of the night, after you've already drunk, won't pull alcohol back out of your bloodstream or lower your blood alcohol in any meaningful way. Only time does that.

### What about late-night food?

A late-night snack after drinking can help a bit if you haven't eaten much, mainly by giving your body some carbohydrate and salt before bed and slowing absorption of any drinks still in your stomach. Something like toast, a sandwich, or a bowl of noodles is a reasonable choice, along with a big glass of water. If you've noticed you get very hungry after drinking, our guide on [why alcohol makes you hungry](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-hungry) explains what's going on.

## Foods and Drinks to Avoid With a Hangover

Some foods make a hangover worse, mostly by irritating a stomach that's already inflamed.

- **Very greasy or heavy food.** Slows stomach emptying and can worsen nausea and reflux, as covered above.
- **Spicy food.** Capsaicin, the compound that makes chili hot, can irritate an already inflamed stomach lining. Save the hot sauce until you're feeling better.
- **Very acidic food and drink.** Lots of orange juice, tomato juice, or vinegar-heavy food can sting if your stomach is sore. Small amounts are usually fine.
- **More alcohol.** A "hair of the dog" drink only postpones the hangover, and it adds to the load on your body. Our guide on [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work) explains why.
- **Huge amounts of sugar on an empty stomach.** A little sugar helps. A giant soda and a pastry on nothing else can leave you crashing an hour later.
- **Lots of caffeine.** Your usual cup is fine. Several energy drinks can make shakiness, a racing heart, and anxiety worse.

If you have stomach pain that's more than mild, our [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) guide covers what's normal and what isn't.

## Hangover "Superfoods" and Viral Food Cures, Checked

You'll find lots of specific foods promoted as hangover cures online. Here's an honest look at the most common ones.

**Korean pear juice.** One of the few foods with a small human study behind it, but the benefit only showed up when people drank it before alcohol, not the morning after. See our [Korean pear juice](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) guide.

**Asparagus.** A lab study on asparagus extracts found they affected enzymes involved in breaking down alcohol in cells. That's a cell-level finding. There is no good evidence that eating asparagus helps a hangover in people.

**Pickles and pickle juice.** Salty, which helps with fluid. Acidic, which may not help your stomach. Fine in small amounts.

**Chocolate.** A craving for sweet things after drinking is common and partly reflects low blood sugar. A little chocolate is harmless, but it's not a treatment.

**Raw egg "prairie oyster" drinks.** Skip them. Raw eggs carry a small risk of salmonella, and there's no benefit over a cooked egg.

**Activated charcoal.** Not a food, but often lumped in. Charcoal binds poorly to alcohol, and there is no good evidence it helps a hangover.

For a broader look at popular online cures, see our guide to [viral hangover cures tested against the science](/never-hungover/viral-hangover-cures-tested-science-2025).

## Do Vitamins in Food Matter?

Heavy drinking can lower levels of some vitamins and minerals over time, including B vitamins (especially thiamine and folate), zinc, and magnesium. A single night out won't leave a healthy person deficient, but a generally good diet may make a difference at the margins. One small observational study from a Dutch-led hangover research group found that people with higher dietary intake of zinc and nicotinic acid (a form of vitamin B3) reported somewhat less severe hangovers. That shows an association, not cause and effect, and it was based on people's own food records.

Practically, that's another argument for ordinary, varied food: eggs, whole grains, beans, nuts, seeds, meat or fish, and vegetables. Our [vitamins for hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) guide covers the supplement side, and our [magnesium guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-hangover-hangxiety-glycinate-vs-citrate-2026) explains that mineral in more detail.

## How Fast Will Food Make You Feel Better?

Food isn't a fast fix. Carbohydrates can lift shakiness and fogginess within 30 minutes to an hour if low blood sugar was part of the problem. Fluid and salt from broth or an electrolyte drink can help a dehydration headache over a few hours. Most of the rest of a hangover, especially fatigue and the general unwell feeling, clears with time, usually within 24 hours.

If you feel worse after eating, or you can't keep anything down at all, stop trying to eat and focus on small sips of fluid. If you still can't keep fluids down after several hours, that's the point to get medical help.

## The Simplest Hangover Food Plan

1. **Right away:** water or an electrolyte drink, in small sips if you're nauseous.
2. **First food (30 to 60 minutes later):** toast, crackers, a banana, or plain rice.
3. **Mid-morning:** broth, soup, or oatmeal for more fluid, salt, and steady carbs.
4. **When appetite returns:** eggs, yogurt, or another gentle protein with carbs.
5. **Later meals:** something balanced with vegetables, like rice with greens and chicken, or avocado toast with eggs.
6. **Avoid for now:** heavy grease, hot spice, more alcohol, and too much caffeine.

## Preventing Next Time: Food Before and During Drinking

Food works better before drinking than after. A real meal with protein, fat, and fiber before you start drinking slows absorption and makes it easier to pace yourself. Snacking during the night, alternating drinks with water, and stopping a few hours before bed help too. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also add a supplement before drinking. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab research, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and it doesn't replace food, water, or drinking less. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- No food cures a hangover, but the right foods help with low blood sugar, fluid loss, and an upset stomach.
- Start with fluids, then bland carbs like toast, crackers, rice, or a banana.
- Broth and soup are the best all-round choice when you feel rough.
- Eggs and other gentle proteins make a good breakfast once your stomach settles.
- Greasy food helps before drinking, not after, and can make nausea and reflux worse.
- Skip spicy food, more alcohol, and heavy caffeine until you feel better.
- Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down, vomit blood, have severe stomach pain, or someone is confused or hard to wake.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best food to eat for a hangover?**

There is no single best food, but bland carbohydrates (toast, crackers, oatmeal, rice), salty fluids like broth or soup, potassium-rich foods like bananas, and gentle protein like eggs cover the main problems a hangover causes: low blood sugar, fluid loss, and an irritated stomach. Start small with fluids and dry carbs, then build up to a proper meal once your stomach settles. No food cures a hangover, but these make the morning easier.

**What should I eat when I'm hungover and nauseous?**

Start with small sips of water, an electrolyte drink, or weak ginger tea. If that stays down for 20 to 30 minutes, try a few crackers, dry toast, plain rice, applesauce, or half a banana. Avoid greasy, spicy, or acidic food until the nausea passes. If you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, or you vomit blood, get medical help.

**Does greasy food help a hangover?**

Not really, at least not the morning after. Fatty food eaten before or while drinking slows alcohol absorption, which can help. Once the alcohol is already absorbed, there is no good evidence that grease speeds recovery, and fatty food can make nausea and acid reflux worse. If a bacon-and-egg sandwich sits well with you, the eggs, bread, and salt still do some good.

**Are bananas good for a hangover?**

Yes, as an easy, gentle food. A medium banana has roughly 400 to 450 mg of potassium plus quick carbohydrates, and it's one of the easiest foods to eat when you feel queasy. The idea that a hangover is mainly a potassium shortage is overstated, so a banana helps more as gentle fuel than as a fix.

**Are eggs good for a hangover?**

Eggs are a good hangover breakfast. They are high in protein, easy to cook gently, and contain cysteine, an amino acid the body uses to make glutathione and to help clear acetaldehyde. A small trial found benefits from an L-cysteine supplement, but there is no good evidence that eating eggs makes a hangover shorter. Think of them as a smart recovery meal, not a treatment.

**What foods should I avoid with a hangover?**

Go easy on very greasy or heavy food, spicy food, very acidic food and juices, large amounts of sugar on an empty stomach, lots of caffeine, and more alcohol. These either irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed or postpone recovery. Your usual cup of coffee is fine, since skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache.

**Does bread soak up alcohol?**

No. Bread doesn't absorb alcohol like a sponge. Eating before or during drinking slows absorption because food keeps alcohol in your stomach longer. Eating bread after you've finished drinking won't pull alcohol out of your bloodstream or lower your blood alcohol in any meaningful way. Only time does that.

**Is soup good for a hangover?**

Yes. Broth-based soup is one of the best things to eat with a hangover. It's mostly water, it brings sodium that helps your body hold onto fluid, and it's warm and gentle on an upset stomach. Chicken noodle soup, bone broth, miso soup, pho, and ramen are all popular choices around the world.
